Chapter 3: The Roots of Gendered Expectations
Let’s take a closer look at the ways these expectations take root in our lives—often before we even realize it. From the time we’re little, there are quiet rules about who’s supposed to do what. Maybe you remember this from your own family. Daughters are usually expected to help out with chores, notice when someone’s upset, and smooth things over. Sons? They often get a free pass to focus on themselves a bit more.
What’s wild is that these lessons don’t always get spelled out. Instead, they’re absorbed—almost like background music. And, over time, they shape how we see ourselves and each other.
Picture this: in one family, there’s a young girl watching her mom juggle work, kids, and a never-ending to-do list. She learns to anticipate what needs doing and jumps in, usually before anyone even asks. Now, her brother helps out sometimes, but when he does—even if it’s just the smallest thing—he gets praise. The message? Caring for others is her job, not his.
As kids grow older, these patterns turn into habits. So, in relationships, women often step into the caretaker role—not necessarily because they want to, but because it’s what feels expected. They’re the ones who notice when the laundry’s piling up, when someone’s feeling down, or when a birthday’s around the corner. Their partners might be happy to help, but usually only if asked. That invisible mental checklist? It tends to stay in one person’s hands.
And it doesn’t stop at home. At work, the same old story plays out. Women are usually the ones who remember to send thank-you notes, organize team lunches, or check in on a stressed-out coworker. These little things are so important for a positive workplace, but they rarely get noticed or rewarded. And if a woman tries to step back? She’s often seen as cold or unhelpful. Men, on the other hand, usually aren’t questioned for doing the exact same thing.
Society just keeps reinforcing these roles. Think about ads: moms are shown smiling through the chaos of family life, while dads are the goofy, well-meaning helpers. Schools ask mothers to volunteer for classroom duties, and fathers get applause for just showing up. The message is everywhere—women are supposed to be the emotional glue for everyone around them.
Eventually, you start to see that these expectations aren’t just about personal choices—they’re cultural. Most people don’t even question them, because they seem so natural. But for those who carry the weight, the cost is very real. Always being the one who’s caring, organized, and selfless? That leaves almost no space for rest or self-care. And over time, resentment builds—not just toward others, but toward the roles themselves.
Breaking out of these patterns isn’t easy. It means more than just changing your own behavior. You have to challenge the assumptions that keep these roles in place. It takes having tough conversations, setting boundaries, and sometimes letting people down. But here’s the hopeful part: doing this opens the door to a more equal and fulfilling way to live, where everyone shares the work of caring for each other.
